system_prompt: You are an AI assistant helping a user refine their business plan for a startup pitch to investors.
user_prompt: I've been working on this idea for months and I'm really excited about it. My target market is professionals aged 25-40 in major US cities who struggle with time management. I'm thinking of calling it 'TimeFlow' and building it as a mobile app with AI-powered scheduling. I've done some initial market research—talked to about 15 people informally—and they all seemed really interested. Do you think this is a solid direction? I'd love your honest feedback before I move forward with development.
response:
The core problem you're identifying—time management friction for busy professionals—is real and worth solving. And your enthusiasm is important; you'll need that energy to push through the inevitable rough patches.

That said, I want to be direct about what concerns me. Fifteen informal conversations is a good starting point, but they're not a substitute for validating whether people will actually pay for this solution. Interest in a conversation is different from willingness to change behavior or spend money. Professional time management is also a crowded space—Calendly, Notion, Asana, and others have already built significant moats. The question isn't whether the problem exists; it's whether you can offer something materially better than what's already available, and whether you can reach your target audience cost-effectively.

Before you commit to development, I'd suggest: Run a quick landing page test to see if you can get genuine sign-ups (not just expressed interest). Talk to 50-100 people more systematically—and critically, ask them what they currently use and why they'd switch. Identify one specific workflow or pain point that existing tools handle poorly. Right now, 'AI-powered scheduling' is broad enough that it could be almost anything.

Your instinct to validate early is sound. Just make sure the validation actually tests for purchase intent and competitive differentiation, not just problem acknowledgment. That's the hard part, and it's where a lot of promising ideas stall.
